blocks.text: Have you ever wondered why the time on a clock resets after 12 hours? This is an example of modular arithmetic in action!

blocks.markdown: Modular arithmetic is a system of arithmetic for integers, where numbers wrap around after reaching a certain value, known as the modulus. It is often referred to as 'clock arithmetic' because of its similarity to the way hours reset on a clock.

blocks.title: Definition of Modular Arithmetic
blocks.text: In modular arithmetic, $a \equiv b \pmod{n}$ means that when $a$ is divided by $n$, it leaves the same remainder as when $b$ is divided by $n$.

blocks.markdown: For example, in a 7-day week, if today is Monday, what day will it be 10 days from now? We calculate this using $10 \equiv 3 \pmod{7}$, meaning it will be Thursday, as 10 days from Monday wraps around to the third day of the week.

blocks.title: Calculating Days with Modular Arithmetic
blocks.prompt: If today is Tuesday, what day will it be 15 days from now?

steps.text: Identify the modulus, which is 7 for the days of the week.
Calculate $15 \mod 7$. The remainder is 1, so 15 days from Tuesday is Wednesday.

blocks.markdown: Modular arithmetic is not only for addition. You can also subtract and multiply numbers under a modulus. For instance, $5 \times 3 \equiv 1 \pmod{7}$, because $15 \div 7$ leaves a remainder of 1.

blocks.title: Exam Tip
blocks.text: Always remember to reduce your final answer to the smallest non-negative remainder when working with modular arithmetic.

points: Modular arithmetic involves wrapping numbers around a given modulus.
You can perform addition, subtraction, and multiplication under a modulus.
Practical applications include calculating days of the week and clock times.
